title: Distance Learning in Numbers
author: Norma Sancho
summary: Norma Sancho synthesizes UNESCO global enrollment data and U.S. postsecondary statistics to provide a quantitative picture of distance learning's reach and its continuing challenges. The key finding: 53.8% of U.S. postsecondary students now take at least one distance course, making online education the statistical norm rather than the exception. Globally, UNESCO data shows enrollment in distance programs has grown fastest in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, where distance education represents the only viable path to credential attainment for most working adults. However, the data also show persistent completion rate disparities: online students complete degrees at lower rates than in-person students even when controlling for demographic and economic factors, with the gap largest for first-generation students and students from low-income backgrounds. The piece is careful to distinguish between the enrollment success of distance education (getting students into programs) and the completion challenge (getting them through to credential), and argues that the field's next decade of improvement needs to focus on the latter.
points: * 53.8% of U.S. postsecondary students now take at least one distance course, making online education the statistical norm rather than the exception -- a threshold crossed with little public acknowledgment. * Global distance education growth is fastest in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, where it represents the only viable credential path for working adults -- making completion rate disparities in those regions a equity issue of significant scale. * Persistent completion rate gaps -- online students complete at lower rates than in-person students even controlling for demographics -- are largest for first-generation students and students from low-income backgrounds, the populations distance education is most supposed to serve. * The data distinguish between enrollment success (which distance education has demonstrated) and completion success (which remains the field's primary unresolved challenge) -- a distinction that summary statistics often obscure. * The implication for institutional investment is that the access problem in online education has largely been solved; the completion problem has not, and the next decade of improvement should focus disproportionately on persistence supports for at-risk online students.
quotes: We passed a threshold quietly. The majority of U.S. postsecondary students now take at least one online course. Online education is not an alternative pathway. It is the pathway. The majority pathway. And yet we still discuss it as if it were a supplement to the real thing.

The UNESCO data for sub-Saharan Africa should stop us. In several countries, distance enrollment is not a minority choice -- it is the only realistic option for a working adult who wants a degree. When we talk about completion rates as a distance-education problem, we are talking about an equity problem at global scale.

The completion rate gap does not close when you control for income and first-generation status. It shrinks, but it doesn't close. There is something about online delivery -- probably the absence of the ambient support structures that in-person campuses provide -- that produces worse completion outcomes independently of who the student is.

Enrollment success is not mission success. A student who enrolls in an online program and doesn't complete has not been served by online education. They have been recruited by it. Those are not the same thing, and institutions that count enrollments as evidence of access are measuring the wrong thing.

The field's next decade of improvement has a clear target. We know how to get students into online programs. We do not know how to get them through with the same reliability as in-person programs. That is a persistence problem, a support structure problem, a belonging problem. It is not an access problem. We solved access.
